item.title: Ben Waters on the latest wireless charging strategies
item.dc:creator: Mike Oitzman
item.description:
Ben Waters discusses opportunity charging, battery life, and the infrastructure needed to keep growing robot fleets running.

The post Ben Waters on the latest wireless charging strategies appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
Wireless chargers are being deployed in a number of indoor and outdoor applications for charging the mobile robots. | Credit: WiBotic

As robot fleets scale, charging becomes an operational challenge. Understanding how to optimize charging for fleets of mobile robots is key to getting the best performance from the fleet throughout the day.

Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic

With growing deployments, charging is becoming more than a question of how long a battery lasts or how quickly it can recharge. Charging strategy can affect fleet uptime, facility infrastructure, maintenance requirements, and even the size of the batteries that robot manufacturers need to carry.

Ben Waters, CEO of WiBotic, recently joined The Robot Report Podcast to discuss how those considerations are changing as robot fleets scale.

He also discussed opportunity charging, the tradeoffs around fast charging, WiBotic’s move toward higher-power systems, and how charging data could help operators identify power problems.

This is an excerpt from the podcast interview. Listen to the full audio anywhere you get your podcasts or online in the show notes.

WiBotic expands beyond its traditional robotics markets

What has changed recently at WiBotic, and how is the market maturing?

Waters: Overall, WiBotic has diversified into a few different markets, but all the while, robotics has really been growing, as we all know, over the last last one to two years for sure.

That was a big motivator for us to pursue getting into some adjacent markets. Take, for example, floor care, medical carts, space, and defense applications, all of which are markets that really use the same product as our longstanding robotics customers from a wireless charging, autonomous charging perspective.

Flash-forward a year of focusing on that and putting all the internal operational, sales, and engineering teams in place to support different markets. Here we are a year and a half later, and robotics is booming everywhere you look, right? I mean, all of our legacy customers in robotics have had significant volume growth this year.

We are seeing huge growth in automotive AMR adoption. We are seeing growth in outdoor robotic inspection for energy substations, and a lot of outdoor applications are growing. And then there’s the wild card of humanoids.

Wireless charging is a really interesting dynamic in humanoids as far as what it can enable and how it can improve uptime and eliminate some of these Achilles’ heels issues that humanoids have around downtime.

Opportunity charging changes the equation for large robot fleets

As fleets of mobile robots grow, where does charging start creating operational friction?

Waters: The big trend as charging relates to operational impact is what we’ve probably talked about before with Gene [Demaitre]. WiBotic has always looked at as a great opportunity for wireless charging. But, you know, it takes a while for fleets to get big enough for it to truly make sense. And I think we’re finally at that place. And what I’m referring to is opportunity charging.

So it’s the concept of “Don’t just put the chargers on the sides of the factories.” And then when the battery on the robot gets to 20%, that robot might be on the far side of the factory. Now it’s got to drive 10 minutes while watching out for everything else and while being ignored by the fleet management for doing a task, even though it’s in an area where a task needs to get done, right? Because it has to go charge.

That strategy, which is arguably easier to implement at a small scale, because you can truly just say, “If any one of these robots’ batteries hits 20%, stop and go drive to the charging station.” That’s fairly easy to implement. That gets really complicated, and that leads to a lot of unwanted downtime when the fleets start to get bigger. Even like fleets of 20 to 40, this becomes a bottleneck.

We need to implement opportunity charging. And it doesn’t make sense to do opportunity charging with anything but wireless. Because if you did it with contacts, your robots would be hitting the contacts so many more times. And even if you had the world’s most strongest contact, it still would require maintenance at some point, times all of the chargers in your fleet.

If the robot does a task and it’s got 10 seconds to sit there, well, a charging station should be positioned right where that robot naturally is going to sit.

You could look at that as well. It’s only charging for 10 seconds, but if you do that often enough, it’s adding substantial energy back into the batteries across the fleet and allowing these things to run 24/7.

You can completely eliminate that. Just allow the robots to stay in the loops where they’re operating when you employ opportunity charging. So that’s really the trend that we’ve been seeing and the demand we’ve been getting, and the main reason why companies are looking for wireless power.

Submit your innovation now!

Charging should be part of the robot design process

How should companies think about charging during system design instead of treating it as an accessory at the end?

Waters: If I boil it down to three things, I think companies should be thinking about power infrastructure. I’ll come back to a few details on these. Where are your electrical outlets, and how many of them do you have, and are they rated for enough power to handle all the chargers you want to deploy? So think about that up front. That bites people. We’ve seen a lot when you think about that too late.

I think people are really questioning. How big of a battery do I need? Do I need a battery that supports an eight-hour runtime? Do I need a battery that supports super fast charging? In the world of batteries, most of these types of things trade off with each other.

They might be overdesigning it. They might be adding way too much battery cost for what they really need, especially if they’re thinking about charging strategies.

We still hear a lot of customers be like, “We need to charge these things as fast as humanly possible.” And we’re going to listen, and we’re going to assume the customers made the right choices for the right reasons.

But sometimes, we do have a strong relationship with someone, we get into these topics. It’s not our job necessarily to push back, but we are curious battery guys, and we’re a friendly company to work with. So we sometimes ask: “Do you really want to charge at 3°C all the time? Have you seen a data sheet from the battery manufacturer that says what that’s gonna do to lifetime? Is that worth it?”

And then the third thing for sure is maintenance. If you wait till you’ve already finished your design, and you’re starting to deploy and haven’t thought about those things, then almost surely, you will get bit by every one of those things within at least a couple of months, if not sooner.

WiBotic develops chargers for outdoor robots, drones and humanoids

As WiBotic moves into new applications, how have its products evolved?

Waters: WiBotic has always really tried to think about what product serves the maximum number of customers and people, right? We’re not a consulting business where we customize every system.

As far as developing circuits and certifying systems, we want to be a company that makes standard products and sells systems to customers that they can depend on that are supported and certified.

We most recently launched in our 1 kW product family an IP65-rated version of the charger. When we first launched our 1 kW product a couple years ago, it was just available in our typical black box IP20 form factor.

So we now have an IP65 form factor, which is really needed for outdoor applications and robotics. Really desirable from, you know, indoor applications like floor care where water and dust are very much parts of those systems.

Right now, we are actively developing more around two areas of innovation. One is size and weight. We are seeing a lot of interest in drone applications. WiBotic certainly has had a long history with drones.

We’re developing lightweight, high-power systems for drones, which just so happens to be kind of the same thing that humanoids need as well.

The more mass you add to a humanoid, the more energy it has to spend because it’s balancing that mass. And there’s not a lot of space. So yeah, we’re focusing on a lot of small form-factor, high-power applications, as well as pushing the power of our current products up to a 3 kW level.

item.title: New ISO interoperability standard covers collaboration among mobile robots from multiple vendors
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
The ISO 21423:2026 interoperability standard is intended to allow mobile robots from multiple vendors to communicate and coordinate.

The post New ISO interoperability standard covers collaboration among mobile robots from multiple vendors appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
The new ISO 21423:2026 standard is intended to facilitate communications among different mobile robots. Source: mansyupasara AI, Adobe Stock

As fleets of mobile robots grow, the need for interoperability among systems increases. The Association for Advancing Automation, or A3, yesterday published ISO 21423:2026, a new international standard for communications among industrial mobile robots, or IMRs, regardless of vendor or model.

“Companies want to choose the robots that fit their applications and have those robots work together on the same floor,” stated Carole Franklin, director of standards development for robotics at A3. “Many leading industrial users of mobile robots have asked for an interoperability standard for years.”

“Now, ISO 21423 gives manufacturers and users a common basis for communication across fleets, no matter where in the world their facility is located,” she added. “This standard can help companies expand automation with equipment from different vendors and make better use of the robots they already have.”

ISO 21423 addresses IMR interoperability

Developed by ISO Technical Committee 299, ISO 21423 Robotics – Industrial mobile robots – Communications and interoperability provides a common set of requirements for automated guided vehicles (AGVs), autonomous mobile robots (AMRs), and similar systems from different suppliers operating in the same facility.

The new standard specifies how IMRs, fleet managers, and other equipment exchange information and request actions. Robots can share their location, speed, direction, condition, tasking and availability with one another, A3 explained.

For end users, this means fewer cases of robots interfering with each other’s paths or path planning, which improves robot availability and system efficiency, asserted A3. A common protocol could increase competition in the market and support innovation, it said. One benefit of an ISO standard on this topic is that it can be adopted in countries all around the world.

Submit your innovation now!

Standard also covers communications with other systems

ISO 21423 also covers communication with machines tended by robots; enterprise resource planning (ERP) tools; and industrial building systems such as lifts, automated doors, and alarms. People using or wearing mobile devices can share similar information, so their work can be coordinated alongside the robots.

“ISO 21423 represents the first non-safety robot standard that A3 has helped produce, and highlights A3’s continued leadership in robotics standardization efforts,” said the Ann Arbor, Mich.-based organization. The standard is available at the A3 online store for $373. A3 members can purchase the document for $320.

The Association for Advancing Automation is a leading global advocate for the benefits of automating. Members of A3 represent more than 1,500 manufacturers, component suppliers, systems integrators, end users, academic institutions, research groups, and consulting firms.

A3 hosts events including the International Robot Safety Conference, the A3 Business Forum, and Automate.

item.title: Churchill Capital XI shareholders approve $2.5B Agility Robotics humanoid SPAC
item.dc:creator: Steve Crowe
item.description:
Deal is expected to provide approximately $465 million in gross capital as Agility expands deployments of its Digit humanoid with industrial customers.

The post Churchill Capital XI shareholders approve $2.5B Agility Robotics humanoid SPAC appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
Digit 5 includes redesigned legs and new batteries for commercial use. Source: Agility Robotics

Agility Robotics has cleared a major hurdle in its planned initial public offering (IPO). Shareholders of Churchill Capital Corp XI approved the special purpose acquisition company’s (SPAC) proposed business combination with the humanoid developer, moving Agility closer to becoming a publicly-traded company.

More than 84% of votes cast at a special shareholder meeting on Nov. 2 supported the deal. The SPAC is expected to close on Nov. 4. The combined company is expected to begin trading on the Nasdaq on Nov. 5 under the ticker symbol AGLT. Churchill Capital stock finished up nearly 14% on Nov. 2. 

The transaction is expected to provide Agility with approximately $465 million in gross capital before expenses. That funding will support commercial expansion, customer deployments and manufacturing capacity as the company looks to scale its Digit humanoid robot business.

The revised capital figure reflects a reduction from the more than $620 million in gross proceeds anticipated when the merger was announced in June. Following the expiration of Churchill XI’s shareholder redemption deadline, the companies now expect approximately $164 million from Churchill’s trust account, approximately $201 million from a private investment in public equity (PIPE) financing led by Foxconn, and $100 million in equity funding Agility received following the initial SPAC announcement.

The original transaction valued Agility at a $2.5 billion pre-money equity value. Existing Agility shareholders will roll their equity into the combined company rather than receive cash in the transaction.

Agility is entering the public markets with more than a proposed product roadmap. Its Digit robots are already operating in 9 customer environments, with logistics and manufacturing emerging as the company’s primary commercial markets.

One of its most established relationships is with GXO Logistics. The companies began working together in 2023 and signed a multi-year Robots-as-a-Service agreement in 2024 to deploy Digit at GXO’s facility in Flowery Branch, Ga. There, Digit has worked alongside existing automation to move totes and place them onto conveyors.

In October, the companies announced an expansion to two additional GXO facilities: Statesville, N.C., and Lebanon, Tenn. Digit will initially support repetitive material-handling tasks in e-commerce fulfillment operations. Deployments are expected to begin in early 2027 using Digit 4, with plans to transition to the newer Digit 5 as it becomes commercially available.

Agility is also moving into manufacturing. In October, agricultural equipment maker AGCO signed a commercial agreement to pilot Digit at its Hesston, Kan., production facility beginning in 2027. Initial tasks will include sorting and stacking parts and placing totes for storage.

Submit your innovation now!

Agility has previously claimed it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5, its next-generation humanoid unveiled in September. The company says early access for customers is expected to begin in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of that year.

That order figure is an important indicator of customer interest, but it should not be confused with current revenue. The multi-year value is expected to be realized over time and remains subject to contractual milestones, product features and specifications.

Agility’s RoboFab manufacturing facility in Salem, Ore., is designed for annual production capacity of up to 10,000 robots. The company is also expanding its software, deployment and service capabilities, including through its Agility Arc fleet-management platform.

item.title: Tutor Intelligence raises Series B to scale model training, robot deployments
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Tutor Intelligence has raised funding to further develop its picking robots, networked intelligence, and commercial deployments.

The post Tutor Intelligence raises Series B to scale model training, robot deployments appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
Tutor trains its Sonny robot on real-world manipulation tasks. Credit: Eugene Demaitre

Real-world data, human “tutors,” and simulation are all part of the recipe for training AI models to enable next-generation robots to tackle a widening variety of tasks. Tutor Intelligence Inc. today said it has raised $75 million in Series B funding as it works toward general-purpose robotics.

“It’s not only that Tutor’s models let robots do jobs that robots have never been able to do before,” stated Josh Gruenstein, co-founder and CEO of Tutor Intelligence. “This type of intelligence also makes robots affordable on a whole new level. We’re unlocking much broader access to the solutions that businesses need to survive and that make basic goods cheaper for everybody. And the demand is there. We can hardly build robots fast enough.”

Tutor Intelligence spun out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (MIT CSAIL) in 2021. The Watertown, Mass.-based company asserted that it is building a full technology stack to “close the gap between what robots can do and what people can do.”

Data flywheel accelerates robot deployment

“Artificial intelligence has transformed the digital world, learning to converse and code from the internet’s vast record of text and images,” said Tutor Intelligence. “The physical world has no such record to train on, and AI has yet to transform it in the same way.”

The company has deployed fleets of internet-connected robots into production environments, where they do real work for customers with input from remote operators known as “tutors.” It uses the real-world data to train better frontier models, ultimately making the robots more capable.

Tutor claimed that its “full-stack platform” and “data flywheel” accelerate deployment, making robots more scalable, safer, and more affordable. Instead of a robots-as-a-service (RaaS) model, business pay Tutor by the hour or by the pick, the same way they pay for manual labor.

Customers make no upfront purchase and sign no long-term contract, added Tutor. The company said it handles deployment and maintenance and regularly sends software and intelligence upgrades. Tutor said its approach is bringing automation to tasks that have long defied conventional, deterministic robotics. It opened a “Data Factory” earlier this year to evaluate policies across 100 physical robots.

Submit your innovation now!

Tutor Intelligence gets traction with Sonny and Cassie

Tutor’s Data Factory includes the Sonny two-armed, semi-humanoid robots for each picking. Cassie is a mobile manipulator designed for case picking and palletizing.

The company reported that twice as many of its robots are working in almost four times as many facilities as a year ago. It said it is on track to have more than 1,000 robots under contract by the end of 2027, all of which will be built in and deployed from the U.S. (The tutors may be overseas.)

The robots are currently moving, lifting, and manipulating objects across some of the country’s largest manufacturing and logistics networks. They handle breakfast cereals, snacks, candy, cosmetics, home goods, toys, and more.

Tutor noted that its growth reflects maturing enterprise adoption of physical AI, as companies move from pilots to expectations of a return on investment from automating their operations. Nearly a third of organizations that received Tutor robots in the past 12 months were existing customers installing more robots, it said.

Funding to support more training and manufacturing

Andreessen Horowitz led Tutor Intelligence’s Series B round, which brings its total capital raised to $117 million. Union Square Ventures and Neo, which led the company’s Series A and seed rounds, respectively, also participated.

“Tutor’s insight is that deployment isn’t just the destination for robotics research—it’s how you overcome its limitations,” said Raghu Raghuram, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz and former CEO of VMware.

“Rather than asking the real world to fit the research, Tutor starts with what real-world deployments demand and works backward through distribution, hardware and research,” he added. “Continual learning across an expanding range of deployments is the path from specialized capabilities to general-purpose robotics.”

Tutor said its latest investment its frontier robot foundation model training, as well as manufacturing and deployment of Sonny and Cassie. It announced the latest models of its robots and underlying platform last month.

item.title: Gentherm designs ThermAffyx to secure, heat patients during robotic surgeries
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
ThermAffyx addresses secure positioning and heating of patients for robot-assisted surgical procedures with a minimal OR footprint.

The post Gentherm designs ThermAffyx to secure, heat patients during robotic surgeries appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
ThermAffyx both securely positions and warms patients during robot-assisted surgeries. Source: Gentherm

Many healthcare advances come from within that industry, but innovations from other industries can also find a role. Gentherm Medical has designed its ThermAffyx Patient Safety System based on thermal management experience from the automotive industry.

The system both securely positions a patient and provides patient warming for robot-assisted surgery. Gentherm Inc. said ThermAffyx does both while minimizing the amount of space required and without the need for forced-air equipment.

The Novi, Mich.-based company launched the system at the Association of periOperative Registered Nurses (AORN) Global Surgical Conference this year. Gentherm noted that numerous medical professionals told it that “almost all of their robotics patients are hypothermic.”

Adam Hauke, global director for product strategy and innovation at Gentherm, replied to the following questions from The Robot Report.

Gentherm addresses Trendelenburg challenge

What is the challenge that ThermAffyx addresses, and how are patient positioning and hypothermia handled conventionally?

Hauke: The ThermAffyx Patient Safety System combines active patient warming and secure positioning into a single solution, helping address two critical perioperative challenges: maintaining normothermia and reducing patient movement during surgery.

The current standard of care consists of forced-air warming solutions and a securement pad. Historically, warming and positioning have been addressed independently because, in many surgical procedures, they do not significantly interfere with one another. However, that’s not the case in most robotic-assisted surgeries.

These procedures frequently require patients to remain in Trendelenburg positioning, where the body is tilted head-down to provide surgical access to the pelvis and lower abdomen. Patients may remain in these positions for extended periods while robotic systems are docked and utilized.

This positioning introduces several challenges, including increased pressure and shear forces that can contribute to pressure injuries, the potential for nerve-related complications if positioning is not optimized, and the risk of patient movement or shifting during lengthy procedures. Underbody securement pads are designed to address these positioning challenges.

At the same time, maintaining normothermia becomes more challenging because robotic equipment occupies the physical space that traditional over-body warming solutions must be deployed in. In these situations, clinicians often rely on under-body warming approaches, but they are difficult or impossible to use in robotics because they would interfere with the underbody securement pads used for safely positioning the patient.

Suddenly, warming and positioning are no longer separate considerations. They are competing for the same real estate.

How much do patients move around during surgical procedures?

Hauke: In the routine course of things in the operating room, “patient movement” is not tracked. “Patient movement,” if it is recorded it is done so as “light anesthesia.” It is usually referring to if the patient’s anesthetic wears off prematurely and they move a hand or leg type thing.

No one is measuring anything on the OR table related to patient movement, as everything is under the sterile drape at that point. The only way the surgical team knows if a patient moves, is if there is tension on the robotic instruments typically.

Any unintended patient movement during robot-assisted surgeries can vary greatly based on a number of factors. There are multiple contributing individual factors such as patient weight, height, and body proportions, as well as procedure-based factors such as the patient position, the steepness the OR table is tilted to and whether or not other positioning solutions are used such as stirrups.

If there is a shift related to Trendelenburg, it’s usually noticed by anesthesia as difficult respirations or a drop in capnography. An actual measurable shift in a patient on the OR table doesn’t occur very often and is not currently a recorded stat.

Submit your innovation now!

Is there a weight or size range for the system?

Hauke: The ThermAffyx System is intended for adult patients and has been tested on individuals up to 297 lb. [134.7 kg]. The Pad is designed so that a patient can be positioned anywhere within the heating zone to receive active warming.

The Pad’s safety sensors do not require direct patient contact to function. As always, clinicians should follow their facility’s protocols and guidelines for safe patient positioning.

Does Gentherm’s system require more power than existing setups?

Hauke: No, ThermAffyx runs on standard hospital electrical outlets.

Is there any danger of thermal or electromagnetic interference with certain surgical instruments?

Hauke: We have mitigated the risks of compatibility with other devices as far as possible. The system has been designed and verified to comply with all applicable industry standards and FDA guidance — including compatibility with electrocautery, diathermy, defibrillation equipment, RFID devices, wireless power transfer devices, and 5G cellular networks. Therefore, the risk of thermal or EM interference is low.

However, there is always residual risk of issues occurring. We do not control the design and use of external devices that may be used in combination with ThermAffyx, and thus cannot guarantee other devices have been designed to meet the same standards or that devices are being used per the manufacturer’s labeling.

ThermAffyx moves toward the market

How is the system progressing toward commercialization?

Hauke: Commercialization is well under way. Our teams are in active trials across the country with strong adoption in both new accounts and our legacy Gentherm accounts.

How difficult was it to get U.S. Food and Drug Administration clearance?

Hauke: Although Gentherm is an expert in patient warming devices, gaining FDA clearance for ThermAffyx took careful development planning and execution. This is the first and only all-in-one product to have Class II indications for use for maintaining normothermia and securement.

To ensure the proper steps were being taken, we started the process with a Q-Sub to the FDA to receive their feedback on our claims and validation plan. We then implemented the appropriate design and testing per the FDA feedback to validate our claims.

An additional requirement with the FDA is to prove the usability of your device. The operation of the device must fit flawlessly into clinicians’ regular workflows to ensure the system can be used safely without introducing complexity. Nurses and anesthesiologists provided critical inputs to the design through focus groups, then validated the design in extensive hands-on usability studies.

Does this add to the cost of OR equipment or surgical procedures?

Hauke: While ThermAffyx does add incremental cost for the technology — lower than most capital budget thresholds — the more important consideration is its potential impact on reducing costly downstream complications.

By helping to reduce the risk of unintended perioperative hypothermia, patient movement or pressure related injuries, the system may help avoid adverse events that can increase length of stay, require additional treatment, and drive higher overall costs of care.

In robotic surgery, these procedures are already supported by established reimbursement structures and procedure codes, making this technology a natural fit within the existing surgical workflow.

Will you be selling it directly or through third parties?

Hauke: ThermAffyx is available for purchase through Gentherm’s U.S. contract sales team.

Are there other potential use cases for ThermAffyx and its component technologies?

Hauke: ThermAffyx was specifically designed to address the challenge of maintaining normothermia in patients undergoing minimally invasive and robotic-assisted procedures, particularly in gynecological, urological, or general surgery cases that require patient positioning in tilt.

However, its innovative 3-in-1 design offers benefits that extend well beyond these initial applications.

By integrating warming technology into a pressure redistributing underbody foam pad, ThermAffyx can help support patient temperature management in a wide range of surgical settings where maintaining normothermia can be difficult including orthopedics, cardiovascular, colorectal, and plastics cases.

item.title: Top 10 robotics developments of October 2026
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Last month, we celebrated the 20th anniversary of RoboBusiness, whic is being rebranded to Robotics Summit & Expo West.

The post Top 10 robotics developments of October 2026 appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
October 2026 was a whirlwind month for the robotics industry. Last month, we celebrated the 20th anniversary of RoboBusiness and announced that next year, the show will be rebranded to Robotics Summit & Expo West.

In addition, prominent humanoid robot companies, such as Agility Robotics and Boston Dynamics, announced some major updates.

Here are the 10 most popular articles on The Robot Report in the past month. Subscribe to The Robot Report newsletter and listen to The Robot Report Podcast to stay up to date on the latest robotics news.

10. AGCO to deploy Agility Digit humanoid in Kansas factory

In October 2026, AGCO and Agility Robotics signed a commercial agreement to deploy Agility’s Digit humanoid in AGCO’s manufacturing facility. The U.S. pilot, expected to begin in 2027, will support AGCO’s efforts to create more flexible, intelligent factories, beginning at its site in Hesston, Kan. Read more.

9. Will ‘boring’ robots win in the real world? Why robotic form should follow workflow

Robots have captured our imagination. We have seen humanoids balancing on one leg, doing backflips, folding laundry, and moving smoothly over difficult terrain. This is all behavior that only a few years ago seemed like something out of science fiction. These viral examples matter because they show that embodied AI has reached a new technical stage. Read more.

8. Agility and GXO Logistics plan expanded deployment of Digit humanoid

Agility Robotics and GXO Logistics said they are expanding their partnership to deploy the Digit humanoid robot in GXO sites in North Carolina and Tennessee. Read more.

7. Boston Dynamics gives more insight into its redesigned humanoid hand

Boston Dynamics in October 2026 gave a look at its new humanoid hand. The four-fingered gripper has 13 degrees of freedom, or DoF, and is directly actuated. The company said it designed it for mass production. Read more.

6. Promise Robotics partners with D.R. Horton on physical AI for homebuilding in October 2026

The construction industry is fragmented and has been relatively conservative about adopting new technologies, but physical AI promises to modernize homebuilding. Promise Robotics said it has signed a multi-year agreement with D.R. Horton, which will use its Factory-as-a-Service capabilities to produce more than 1,250 homes in the U.S. Read more.

5. AWS launches open-source Physical AI Toolchain for robotics

Amazon Web Services launched an open-source Physical AI Toolchain designed to help roboticists move from collecting data to training, simulating, validating and deploying AI models on their robots. The toolchain brings together AWS services and NVIDIA’s Physical AI software stack into a single development workflow. Read more.

4. PTC acquisition positions Schneider Electric to challenge Siemens

Global energy company Schneider Electric in October 2026 said it will acquire industrial design, engineering, and data management firm PTC for about $22.6 billion. The Boston-based companies claimed that the combination will bridge the “digital and physical worlds across the lifecycle, from design and build to operate and maintain.” Read more.

3. Boston Dynamics drops pinky on new humanoid hand

Boston Dynamics unveiled the newest hand for its Atlas humanoid in October 2026. The hand is directly actuated, and is designed for mass manufacturing. Previous versions of Atlas’ hand featured seven degrees of freedom and were designed to grasp a large variety of objects, Boston Dynamics said. With the latest hand, the company is shifting its focus to manipulating those objects. Read more.

2. Boston Dynamics appoints former Amazon exec Rohit Prasad as new CEO in October 2026

It has been nearly nine months since Robert Playter, the former CEO of Boston Dynamics, stepped down. The company has named Rohit Prasad as its new CEO. Prasad will take over from Chief Financial Officer Amanda McMaster, who served as interim CEO. Read more.

1. Gecko Robotics secures $300M contract with the U.S. Navy

Gecko Robotics said it has earned an additional $300 million its contract with the U.S. Navy and General Services Administration. With the increase, the U.S. government has quadrupled the ceiling value on Gecko’s contract for slashing maintenance delays and improving fleet readiness. Read more.

The post Top 10 robotics developments of October 2026 appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: What AgTech founders get wrong about ROI
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Connie Bowen, the founding general partner of Farmhand Ventures, discusses the importance of return on investment for AgTech developers.

The post What AgTech founders get wrong about ROI appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
The Robot Report Podcast · What AgTech founders get wrong about ROI

Connie Bowen, founding general partner of Farmhand Ventures.

In Episode 268 of The Robot Report Podcast, our guest is Connie Bowen, the founding general partner of Farmhand Ventures, a venture fund with a focus on AgTech investments.

Farmhand Ventures is an impact-first investment firm shaping the future of work in agriculture. It enables strategic programs and innovation to make farm work more attractive, productive, profitable, and resilient — improving the lives and livelihoods of farmers, farmworkers, and rural communities.

A lifelong ag leader and engineer, Bowen has planted orchards, harvested hemp, and managed farm crews. That experience grounds her investment lens in the realities of the field.

Over the past decade, Bowen has built a career connecting agricultural technology with practical farming needs, holding roles at The Yield Lab, AgLaunch, Chess Ag Full Harvest Partners, and Grape Arbor Ventures before founding Farmhand.

item.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics
item.dc:creator: Sponsored Content
item.description:
VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem.

The post 28 Zero-Day Findings in Less Than Two Days: What AI-Speed Discovery Means for Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.

Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.

Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.

These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.

What AI changes about vulnerability discovery

Vulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.

When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.

Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycle

VicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.

Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.

The following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.

  • Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robot
    A team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly.
  • Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidence
    Importing a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence.
  • Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or control
    An attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly.

These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.

In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.

Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working.

A published patch still needs to be proven safe

AI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.

An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.

Three questions can help teams respond:

  • Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots.
  • What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior.
  • How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended.

When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.

From discovery to safer deployment

As details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.

That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.

Faster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, watch for VicOne’s upcoming white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

item.title: Why physical AI is the next lucrative frontier
item.dc:creator: Janis Skriveris
item.description:
To prove its commercial value, physical AI must get past funding enthusiasm and move into production environments.

The post Why physical AI is the next lucrative frontier appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
Genesis AI recently unveiled the Eno robot to bring physical AI into commercial environments. Source: Genesis AI

The fastest-growing market categories have humble beginnings. Physical AI, the combination of robotics and advanced artificial intelligence, is just the latest example.

ChatGPT began as a pitch deck at an accelerator before it became a household name in 2023. Before cloud computing became a boardroom imperative, founders were building it, server rack by server rack, cluster by cluster. And, of course, before fintech rewired retail banking, it appeared as a funding surge in deal flow data that most banks weren’t reading.

You see the pattern, and I’ve watched it repeat itself across several years of evaluating startups. The startup ecosystem is the world’s most underutilized business intelligence system.

Incumbents may amass wealth and power, but it’s the founders who choose to build. Which sectors attract a sudden surge of founding activity is a three-to-five-year leading indicator of where enterprise disruption is headed.

While AI agents garner the lion’s share of media attention and VC funding, deal flow suggests the next market for hypergrowth will be of the metallic persuasion. That is physical AI, which includes autonomous machines and smart manufacturing, among other sensor-laden systems.

Robotics and physical AI startups raised a record $27.6 billion across 1,009 deals in 2025, or more than double the prior year, according to PitchBook. Genesis AI, which emerged from stealth with a $105 million seed round, recently demonstrated a wheeled robot that can bring physical AI into commercially relevant environments without needing to replicate the human body.

Physical AI: Intelligence inside

Physical AI systems can perceive environments, understand spatial context, make operational decisions, and act autonomously in real time across industrial and other settings. Physical AI systems move beyond static automation toward adaptive operations that continuously improve through interaction with the real world.

As with most tech trends, physical AI is driven by a coalescence of several technologies that have matured simultaneously. These include: multimodal sensing, edge computing, simulation environments, robotics foundation models, and world modeling systems. These technologies allow machines to collect information from the physical environment, interpret it in context, simulate outcomes before acting, and continuously refine performance through operational feedback loops.

In addition, the costs of several components that make physical AI possible have declined, with lidar, actuators, depth cameras, and sensors becoming more affordable.

For example, Waymo said its sixth-generation Driver system significantly reduced costs while increasing resolution, range, and compute power. The autonomous vehicle system used a suite of 13 cameras, four lidars, and six radars. Together, the technological maturation plus cost reduction cultivates the right conditions for physical AI to blossom.

Manufacturing, automotive, logistics, and healthcare sectors have emerged as major areas of capital concentration, with organizations actively piloting robotics to address labor costs and the scarcity of qualified personnel, and deploying them in harsh environments even as productivity needs grow.

Figure AI, whose humanoid robots assemble automobile parts in BMW factories, reached a $39 billion valuation within three years, the fastest path to unicorn status in robotics history. Investors are banking on general-purpose robot models doing for hardware what large-language models did for software. Why wouldn’t they? The deal flow is there.

Three stages of a disruption wave

Throughout the past few years of reading deal flow, I’ve identified a consistent three-stage pattern that plays out across every major technology disruption.

Stage 1: The founder surge

A new capability emerges, attracting a disproportionate number of high-quality founding teams. Capital concentrates. Failure rates soar even as the survivors are defining the category. As I alluded to earlier, generative AI shot to the stars in 2023. Agentic AI is now moving through this stage, while physical AI is just entering it.

Dyna Robotics, which is building foundation models that let one robot learn service tasks for hotels, restaurants, and laundromats, raised a $120 million Series A funding round within about a year of its founding.

Stage 2: The corporate adoption wall

Enterprises begin piloting the technology but struggle to move from experiment to production. The startups that survive stage one hit procurement cycles, integration complexity, and organizational resistance. We’re seeing this right now with organizations implementing GenAI and agentic AI tools without adapting their operating models, according to Deloitte.

Some organizations break through this wall. After recognizing that generative AI would fundamentally reshape customer service, Intercom canceled non-AI projects, reorganized product teams and committed $100 million to replatform the business around AI. That transformation produced its Fin agent which now resolves millions of customer service queries.

Another company, Maven Robotics, mixed palletizing in warehouses, and is crossing the wall one customer at a time.

Stage 3: Industrialization

A subset of companies cracks the deployment code. The technology becomes operational infrastructure. The window for competitive entry is closing. Cloud computing reached this stage around 2015. GenAI and agentic AI will land there within 18 to 24 months, as organizations redesign their processes and double down on their change management practices.

Kiva Systems‘ warehouse robots, bought by Amazon in 2012, grew into a fleet of more than 1 million. What was once a startup capability is now sophisticated infrastructure that new entrants can’t easily match.

The practical implication is straightforward: by the time a technology reaches Stage 3, the structural advantages of early deployers are largely locked in. The companies that used AWS in 2010 to save money eventually built strong engineering cultures, data architectures, and product velocity in the ensuing years.

Submit your innovation now!

Physical AI today, something else tomorrow

The same dynamic is playing out in AI today and the deal flow is telling us exactly which categories are where on that curve. For physical AI, the competitive advantage lies in the ability to build continuous operational learning loops where physical interaction generates data, data improves simulation and models, and improved models enhance real-world performance.

As the deployment of these intelligent systems scales, they compound advantages through infrastructure integration, operational feedback and real-world learning. More data, operationalized appropriately, yields better outcomes.

Most corporate leaders treat startup deal flow as noise. They may discount it as too early-stage, too speculative, or too distant from their operating reality.

But rather than watch startup deal flow to find your next vendor, watch it to understand where the next generation of your competitive environment is being built. Then calibrate your own development and strategic roadmap accordingly. The signals are there; you just need to know how to read them.

About the author

Janis Skriveris is a principal and Plug and Play Ventures and director of its Deeptech Platform. He sources, diligences, and leads investments in deeptech and AI companies shaping the next generation of industrial and urban systems.

Skriveris focuses on applied AI, robotics and autonomy, next-gen mobility, industrial technologies, and the built environment — real estate, construction, and infrastructure. He helps companies validate commercial traction, refine their go-to market strategies, and access Plug and Play’s global corporate network. Since 2017, Skriveris has led 37 investments, including unicorn Einride.

Prior to Plug and Play, Skriveris worked at EY’s Assurance and Consulting Department, where he developed a deep understanding of various industries and honed his skills in strategic planning, risk management, and business transformation. He holds a bachelor’s degree in economics and entrepreneurship, graduating with distinction from the University of Latvia. Janis completed a master’s degree in finance and financial management services at the Faculty of Business, Management and Economics of the same university.

item.title: Solving the Interconnect Challenge in Modern Robotics: How 3M Is Engineering for Motion, Density, and Uptime
item.dc:creator: Sponsored Content
item.description:
As robotics systems grow more capable — faster, more precise, and increasingly reliant on AI-driven vision and control — the humble interconnect is being asked to do more than ever.

The post Solving the Interconnect Challenge in Modern Robotics: How 3M Is Engineering for Motion, Density, and Uptime appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
By Heilind Electronics

As robotics systems grow more capable — faster, more precise, and increasingly reliant on AI-driven vision and control — the humble interconnect is being asked to do more than ever. Signal integrity, mechanical durability, and board real estate are no longer secondary considerations in robotics design; they’re often the limiting factor. 3M has built out a portfolio of connectors, cables, and cable assemblies aimed squarely at these pressure points, and the company’s interconnect strategy for robotics offers a useful lens into where the industry’s hardware challenges are heading.

Flex Life Is the New Uptime Metric

Robotic joints, arms, and end effectors don’t sit still — they twist, bend, and cycle continuously, often for years without a maintenance window. Cabling that fatigues or fails under that mechanical stress is one of the more common causes of unplanned downtime in automated systems.

3M’s answer is a family of high-flex cable assemblies built specifically for motion-intensive applications. CoaXPress-compatible assemblies are flex-cycle tested to 45 million cycles, while USB3 Vision-compatible assemblies push that rating to 100 million cycles. On the flat-ribbon side — used widely for I/O and data runs in robotic subsystems — 3M offers a range spanning roughly 1 million to 100 million flex cycles, giving engineers a way to match cable durability to the actual duty cycle of a given axis or joint, rather than over- or under-engineering the harness.

For machine vision applications specifically, where camera cables are constantly routed through moving linkages, this kind of validated flex-life data lets designers make a real engineering trade-off instead of a guess.

IDC Termination: An Old Idea Still Solving New Problems

3M invented Insulation Displacement Contact (IDC) termination back in 1961, and it remains one of the more underappreciated tools in high-mix robotics manufacturing. Rather than crimping or soldering individual conductors, IDC connectors displace the wire insulation during a single mass-termination step; 3M IDC solutions can save up to 80% in wiring time compared with crimp-style connectors.

That speed advantage compounds in two directions that matter to robotics builders. On the production floor, IDC simplifies mass termination across ribbon cable and multi-conductor harnesses, which is particularly relevant given how much I/O and sensor wiring modern robots carry. In the field, many IDC-based connectors support one-hand mating and unmating, which shortens service windows when a module needs to be swapped on a production line that can’t afford extended downtime.

Board Space Is Getting More Expensive

As robotic controllers and sensor modules pack more compute and I/O into the same footprint, connector real estate has become a genuine design constraint. 3M’s response includes reduced-pitch options like the Cable Socket 451 and Header 452 Series, built at half the pitch of the industry-standard 0.100-inch grid — effectively doubling contact density in the same board area.

For lower pin-count applications — 2- to 4-wire sensor and signal connections that are ubiquitous in robotics — 3M’s Mini-Clamp connectors offer a compact footprint without requiring a full IDC harness, while the Mini Stack header and socket family pushes board footprint reduction even further for designs where every square millimeter counts.

Reliability Under Vibration and Noise

Constant motion brings constant vibration, and vibration is what turns a marginal connection into an intermittent fault. Several of 3M’s connector lines incorporate screw-lock retention specifically to maintain contact integrity in environments where mechanical disturbance is the norm rather than the exception.

EMI and crosstalk are the other reliability variable in dense robotic wiring, where high-speed data lines often run in close proximity to motor and power cabling. 3M offers cable and connector options selected specifically to help manage that interference, which matters increasingly as robots incorporate more real-time vision and sensor fusion.

For applications that need a sealed, one-piece solution rather than a discrete connector-and-cable assembly, 3M’s Molded-On Cable Assemblies provide a ruggedized, fully customizable option — useful where a robot’s environment (washdown, particulate, or extreme vibration) makes a traditional connector interface a liability.

Why This Matters for Robotics Engineers

Flex-tested cables, IDC termination, and reduced-pitch connectors represent the kinds of infrastructure decisions that can influence a robotics platform’s reliability and performance in the field. As robotic systems take on more autonomous, safety-critical, and continuously operating roles, the interconnects tying sensors to controllers to actuators become a real point of engineering leverage rather than an afterthought. 3M’s robotics-focused interconnect lineup, including high-flex cable assemblies, IDC connectors, reduced-pitch board connectors, and molded cable assemblies, gives design engineers a menu of validated options for addressing flex life, assembly time, board density, and long-term reliability. For teams building or specifying the next generation of robotic hardware, that combination of decades of interconnect experience and application-specific testing (like the 45- and 100-million-cycle flex ratings) is worth a closer look during the component selection phase, well before a design freeze locks those decisions in. item.title: Unusual robotic animals can prove their utility
item.dc:creator: Elena Krosheva
item.description:
Robotic animals are designed to be helpful rather than scary, showing promise in disaster recovery, utility inspection, and companionship.

The post Unusual robotic animals can prove their utility appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
Korean researchers have developed a beetle-like soft robot. Source: KAIST

When we hear the word “robot,” we still conjure up images of mechanical figures from old science fiction films. However, reality has long since evolved: We’re surrounded by smart vacuum cleaners, voice assistants, and even four-legged machines that mimic dogs. But what are these robotic animals?

They’re not just battery-powered toys. They’re complex electronic devices, infused with elements of artificial intelligence, that replicate the appearance and behavior of real or imaginary creatures.

These devices contain sensors, speakers, motors, and processor modules that analyze external signals. They’re controlled via mobile apps. Digital pets can make distinctive sounds, respond to signs of affection, answer to their names, and display a range of emotions—from delight to fear, from satisfaction to fatigue.

Manufacturers employ a variety of engineering approaches when creating these devices. Let’s look at some interesting examples.

Microrobot beetle and its relatives

A microrobot beetle might seem like a fun little gadget. But leading research centers such as the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) are working on developing similar insects (see image above).

So why are robot ants, robot beetles, and robot bees being created? The answer lies in solving practical and even humanitarian problems.

Cyborg cockroaches: Rescuers from under the ruins

In the spring of 2022, a tragedy occurred in the city of Changsha, China—a six-story building collapsed. Dozens of people were trapped under the rubble. Many remained missing for nearly six days.

Rescue efforts were hampered by piles of rubble and collapsed floors. Ultimately, 53 people died, and only 10 were rescued. In such operations, every minute is precious. Rescuers use thermal imaging cameras and comb through the rubble, but this takes precious time.

But what if cockroaches come to the rescue? These insects are fast and can penetrate even the tiniest cracks, allowing them to quickly survey the disaster area. But how can they be made to search for people? A team at Nanyang Technological University (NTU) in Singapore said it has found a solution by transforming a Madagascar cockroach into a cyborg.

A miniature backpack containing a microcomputer is attached to the insect’s back. It contains sensors that detect dangerous gas concentrations, as well as an infrared camera with a thermal imager, allowing it to detect bodies under the rubble. To prevent the insects from scattering randomly, but rather to remain confined to a specific area, the scientists have developed a remote control system.

Electrodes and a microchip are attached to the cockroach’s body. An electrical impulse to the right side causes the insect to move to the left, and vice versa. When both electrodes are activated, the cockroach accelerates and runs straight.

This cyborg can operate for long periods in rubble: the microcomputer is powered by solar panels. One individual can survey an area of up to 100 sq. m (1,076.3 sq. ft.). The operator controls the movement and monitors the signals from the sensors.

However, there’s a catch: to fully survey a large building, about 500 of these cockroaches are required, meaning 500 operators. And although the cyborg will indicate the location of the victim, it won’t be able to extract them—that’s a task for humans.

Robot ants: Strength in miniature

Stanford University engineers created mechanical ants capable of moving loads 2,000 times their own mass. For a human, this is the equivalent of moving a 150-ton whale.

Just four of these tiny animals can transport an adult, and a whole group can lift a concrete slab or rebar. This phenomenal lifting capacity was achieved thanks to a gecko-inspired paw design that provides a secure grip on any surface.

A special coating of microscopic rubber hairs creates a bio-stimulated adhesive effect: When the rope is taut, the robot adheres and releases when it is loosened.

However, this high performance requires a lot of energy. The battery can run out at critical moments, so in industrial settings, these ants are connected to a cable and used as towing vehicles.

Snake-like robot: Underwater repairman

Animal robots are capable of not only eliminating the consequences of disasters but also preventing them. Norwegian developers have created a 5 m (16.4 ft.) robotic snake for servicing underwater oil pipelines. It inspects pipelines, transmits images to a dispatcher, and, if a defect is detected, repairs it.

Equipped with manipulators at both ends, the snake can replace valves and clean deposits from pipes. These devices can operate at depths of up to 500 m (1,640.4 ft.) for up to six months, recharging at special stations.

Robot crab: Underground explorer

University of California, Berkeley, engineers developed a robotic crab for underground exploration. Using fabric scoops on its claws, it burrows into the ground, collects samples, and analyzes the soil. Equipped with sensors and a manipulator, it can determine the suitability of a site.

These robotic animals could be used in construction or agriculture, detecting pollution. In the future, such crabs are even planned for use on the Moon. Scientists are currently working on improving the design so that the robot can dig deeper.

More recently, open-source crab platforms are helping developers innovate locomotion.

Robot falcons: Airfield guardians

Mechanical falcons, developed at the University of Groningen in the Netherlands, are already in service in Canada and Germany. They frighten real birds away from runways, preventing collisions that could lead to plane crashes.

Unlike acoustic cannons, which birds quickly become accustomed to, robotic predators exploit natural fear—they not only mimic predators but also pursue live birds, demonstrating dominance.

Robot bee: Space scout

A miniature robotic bee, the size of a pinhead, was created at Harvard University. Although it can theoretically pollinate plants, its true purpose is reconnaissance. Sensors mimic the vision and antennae of insects and transmit a three-dimensional image to the operator.

This micro-reconnaissance vehicle can fly, swim, and dive. It runs on solar batteries, consuming only 120 milliwatts—less than a light bulb. Scientists are confident that these bees will be useful for exploring Martian canals, lunar craters, and even the toxic clouds of Venus.

A variety of zoomorphic robots emerges

Today, numerous robots mimic the behavior of a wide variety of animals. Their advantage is the ability to move horizontally and vertically, navigate obstacles, and penetrate hard-to-reach places.

Unlike real animals or people, they do not require food or water, making them suitable assistants in deserts, mountains, and the exploration of other planets. They could be indispensable in rescue operations and scientific research.

For example, MIT scientists created Mini Cheetah—a platform used to test algorithms for guide robots and jumping machines. Chinese engineers have developed an insect-sized model that has the properties of spiders and cockroaches. Another robotic cheetah from DARPA reached speeds of up to 18 mph.

A flexible robot, modeled after the Caenorhabditis elegans roundworm, was capable of navigating around obstacles. Gecko Robotics has commercially deployed systems equipped with suction cups for vertical movement and can operate in hazardous environments.

Submit your innovation now!

Quadrupeds follow dogs as human companions

Some four-legged robots can travel over 30 km (18.6 mi.) without recharging and carry loads of up to 180 kg (396.8 lb.). They can transport the injured and recognize voice commands.

Three years ago, Moscow State University unveiled the first such robot in Eastern Europe, costing approximately 1.5 million rubles. The Unitree Robotics A1 model, weighing 15 kg (33 lb.), was controlled by powerful electric motors. It was even tested at a zoo to observe the animals’ reactions.

After testing, the design was modified, improving access to the internal subsystems. The robot is controlled by a joystick and connected to cameras and lidar for navigation. Its basic gait is a trot, and its speed is 3.5 km/h. The dog can change its gait, shake a paw, stand up, and lie down.

Unitree introduced the As2 companion earlier this year.

Animal-inspired robots evolve

Although today there are robotic kangaroos, insects, and reptiles, the dog was the first and most common prototype. This is due to the animal’s familiarity as a human assistant. The mechanics of canine movement (walking, running, jumping) proved optimal for engineering solutions. Robo-dogs range in size from a mastiff to a Labrador.

The predecessor is considered to be Phony Pony, a Californian robot from the late 1960s. It didn’t resemble an animal much, but it already had articulated supports, sensors, and motors, becoming the forerunner of all quadrupeds.

Companion animal robots offer therapy and care

Interacting with animals can reduces stress and anxiety. There’s even pet therapy. Pets are especially beneficial for the elderly with dementia, children with mental health issues, and hospital patients.

However, live animals require care, and they are often prohibited in medical facilities. That’s where companion robots come in.

New Zealand scientists have proven that interacting with them is just as beneficial as interacting with real animals. They are hypoallergenic, don’t require food or walking, and their behavior is predictable.

Joy for All

These realistic cats and dogs from Joy for All are covered in soft fur. Cats open their mouths, blink, groom themselves, and roll over when petted. Dogs bark in response to voices, respond to hugs, and their “heartbeat” changes. They fall asleep in the dark. Touch and light sensors are built into the body.

Scientists at Brown University worked on software to transform them into assistants for the elderly. The robotic animals can remind them to take their medications and find their glasses or keys.

Jenny by Tomobot

Tomobot has designed its realistic golden Labrador puppy for the elderly and children with autism. It does not walk to avoid creating a hazard. Jenny senses touch, responds to commands (called “voice”), wags its tail, whines, and snores in its sleep.

The robotic animal contains 50 sensors, 10 motors (seven in its face), and microphones. An app allows users to name the dog and update its settings.

PARO — a harp seal

This robot animal is listed in the Guinness Book of World Records as “the most therapeutic.” Developed in Japan, it promotes relaxation and positive emotions.

The seal pup is covered in sensory whiskers and tactile sensors, moves its paws, makes sounds, recognizes its name, and responds to affection. If ignored, it cries. The charger is shaped like a pacifier, and when removed, PARO makes a disgruntled squeak. Its personality changes depending on how it’s handled.

Aibo by Sony

This sophisticated puppy featured a camera, sensors, and 22 axes of motion. Its eyes are two OLED screens. Thanks to cloud technology, aibo remembered events, developed its personality, and learned.

This robotic dog could play, bark at strangers, patrol a route, and send photos to its owner, although this was primarily for entertainment purposes. Sony discontinued sales of Aibo in June of this year, demonstrating some of the challenges with developing robots for the consumer market.

Robotic animals could become part of our lives

Robot animals are increasingly becoming a part of our lives as therapists, assistants, and friends. They are purchased for children, the elderly, and people with allergies or restrictions on pets.

In Japan, where the problem of an aging population is particularly acute, these devices have long been part of the care system. Europe and the U.S. are also actively investigating them for hospitals and nursing homes, accelerating development. Electronic animals are not just toys, but an important tool for care and rescue.

About the author

Elena Krosheva is a freelance journalist, marketing analyst, and SEO specialist. She graduated with honors from the Faculty of Journalism at the Institute of Modern Knowledge in Minsk, Belarus, in 2007.

Krosheva covers topics such as digitalization, IT, the modern economy, and transhumanism. She loves computers and cyberpunk, having graduated from a technical college before graduating from the Faculty of Journalism.

item.content:encoded:
Operators can start Axion with their existing inspection data and add Percepto’s autonomous systems and managed remote operations wherever more frequent coverage is needed. | Credit: Percepto

Autonomous drone inspection provider Percepto this week launched Axion, a hardware-agnostic physical AI platform that marks the company’s shift to a software-first strategy. The company said it allows critical infrastructure operators to analyze data from any third-party drone or sensor network to prevent equipment failures before they escalate.

Founded in 2014, Percepto said its initial team built the technology needed for scale. The company asserted that its new management has decades of independent experience with growth across robotics, sensors, the Internet of Things (IoT), physical AI, and cybersecurity.

Percepto is based in Modi’in, Israel, with U.S. headquarters in Austin, Texas.

New executives pivot Percepto to software-first strategy

Julien Bellanger recently took the the helm from longtime CEO Dor Abuhasira alongside new revenue and marketing leadership. Percepto said the executive shifts signal its strategic pivot from a hardware-centric autonomous drone maker to a software-first physical AI provider.

“When I looked at Percepto, I saw a company that had already done the hardest part: fully autonomous drones flying real missions every day at some of the most demanding industrial sites in the country,” Bellanger told The Robot Report. “With AIM [Autonomous Inspection & Monitoring] and Axion, we’re taking that operational intelligence beyond our own fleet and opening it to the entire industry.”

The company plans to continue selling, deploying, and supporting its current product line of drones and drone docks. At the same time, manufacturing will be located onshore in the U.S. to support the American Drone Dominance Initiatives.

Submit your innovation now!

Axion extends inspection workflows

Percepto said it has designed the Axion platform to add value to inspection workflows across mission-critical operations, including upstream oil and gas, power transmission and distribution, and most downstream processing facilities.

With Axion, Percepto said it expects to work across the entire industry and to help business grow with AIM’s capabilities. The company is using compliance waivers to control and autonomously fly in one-to-many configurations. Axion will ingest all data sources and provide actionable insights with more than 160 AI models, it claimed.

“The infrastructure powering our economy should benefit from the same advances in AI that are transforming the digital world,” said Bellanger. “Our vision is to provide operators with a trusted understanding of what is happening across their infrastructure, with the foresight to protect the people and operations that depend on it.”

“Axion is the first step in this next chapter, opening our technology to more operators and putting their existing inspection investments to work toward that goal,” he added. “From Day 1, a team can bring the inspection data it already has and see which assets need attention first.”

Available as a software-as-a-service offering, Axion organizes inspection data by asset and applies AI that interprets equipment condition in context. It ingests data from supported third-party drone platforms, fixed and mobile sensors, and existing inspection archives, so operators are not tied to a single hardware provider.

Percept said that Axion can identify a downed wire by its relationship to surrounding components or evaluate a thermal anomaly against expected asset behavior and environmental conditions. Each finding is backed by inspection history and expert validation, giving teams confidence in what needs attention.

In addition, Percepto asserted that Axion enables users to query the corpus of inspection data using plain-language queries. It said its large language model (LLM) enables users to quickly get to the answers that they are seeking and exposes the valuable signals contained in the inspection data.

item.title: Humanoid developer Agility now expects to raise $465M in SPAC deal
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
Agility said it expects to raise $465 million in its combination with Churchill Capital Corp XI, $155 million less than it had estimated.

The post Humanoid developer Agility now expects to raise $465M in SPAC deal appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.content:encoded:
Digit 5 includes redesigned legs and new batteries for commercial use. Source: Agility Robotics

Humanoid robotics developers continue to raise millions of dollars. Agility Robotics Inc. and Churchill Capital Corp XI today said that they expect Agility to raise about $465 million in its proposed merger with the special-purpose acquisition company, or SPAC.

According to Agility, the gross capital raise includes:

  • About $164 million from Churchill XI’s trust account
  • Approximately $201 million from a common stock PIPE (private investment in public equity) committed at $10 per share, led by Foxconn with participation from existing and new institutional investors
  • $100 million of equity funding already received following the announcement of the business combination

That total is less than the $620 million that Agility predicted at a $2.5 billion valuation when it first announced the planned business combination in June. The Robot Report has reached out to the company for comment and will add it if we get a response.

“Agility is expected to enter the public markets well capitalized to execute its planned investments in commercial expansion and support growing customer demand,” stated the Salem, Ore.-based company.

Agility expects to close the SPAC transaction, subject to shareholder approval and the customary closing conditions, on Nov. 4. The company has claimed that it will be the first U.S. publicly traded, pure-play humanoid supplier with commercial deployments.

Agility gets Digit ready for customers

Last month, Agility unveiled its Digit 5 humanoid, which had new legs (and possibly wheels) and is designed to work safely alongside people and support a range of workflows. Last week, Jonathan Hurst, co-founder and chief robot officer, and Pras Velagapudi, chief technology officer at the company, spoke about humanoid advances at RoboBusiness 2026.

Agility this month also chose Nyobolt for fast recharging, which it said will enable its robots to operate for more than 20 hours a day.

The company said it is “on track to begin deliveries to early-access customers in the first half of 2027, with general availability targeted for the end of 2027.” Agility also said it has more than $300 million in committed multi-year orders for Digit 5.

Humanoid use cases are growing

Digit continues to make progress in live operations. In a September S-4 statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Agility reported $1.8 million in net sales in 2025. Its customers across nine sites include Toyota, Mercado Libre, and Schaeffler.

AGCO this month announced plans to deploy Digit in its agricultural machinery factory in Kansas.

And this week, Agility said it is expanding its partnership with GXO Logistics, implementing humanoids in North Carolina and Tennessee.

Humanoid companies continue fundraising, acquisitions

Agility’s investors include NVIDIA (with whom it also expanded its relationship), Amazon, SoftBank Vision Fund 2, Schaeffler, Foxconn, Abico, DCVC, and Playground Global. The company said that all existing shareholders will roll their equity into the combined company and will be subject to a 180-day lock-up at closing.

Some of the top funding rounds for humanoid companies so far this year include Neura Robotics‘ $1.4 billion Series C, XPeng Robotics‘ $900 million Series A, AI2 Robotics‘ $735 million Series C, and Apptronik‘s $520 million Series A-X.

Top acquisitions include UBTECH‘s purchase of Fenglong Electric for $249 million and Faraday Future‘s purchase this week of FF Robotics.
